options.how: Rent storefronts, stock them, hire and schedule staff, import through the harbor into warehouses; HQ managers later automate logistics.
Cities earn gold per turn from tile yields, districts and trade routes; you spend one empire treasury and never run a single shop.

sources.note: Big Ambitions: hands-on open world business sim
Civilization VI: gold per turn from yields, districts and trade routes

options.how: Buy stock in the town markets, set a price for each item on display and haggle with each customer at the counter.
Pop jobs on planets yield energy credits and minerals each month into one empire-wide stockpile; there are no individual shops.

sources.note: Recettear: per-customer pricing and haggling
Recettear: decide how much to sell things for, play the town markets
Stellaris: energy credits and minerals as empire-wide resources

options.how: Order stock on the store computer, unpack it onto shelves, set each product's price, scan items at checkout, then hire staff.
Buy businesses that pay out on timers; hired managers keep them earning while you are away, so money is one growing number.

sources.note: Supermarket Simulator: stock shelves, set prices, take payments, hire staff
AdVenture Capitalist: hire a manager to keep earning while you are gone

options.how: Grind ingredients and steer each brew in the cauldron by hand, then serve customers one at a time at your shop counter.
Buildings bake cookies per second on their own; each purchase raises that building's cost by 15%, so the economy is one rate.

sources.note: Potion Craft: physically interact with tools to brew, customers visit your store
Cookie Clicker: buildings passively generate cookies, cost +15% each

options.how: Put dungeon loot on display tables, set each price yourself and manage gold reserves; recruit an assistant and upgrade the shop.
Monthly ducat income sums province tax, production and trade; you balance a national budget, not individual merchants.

sources.note: Moonlighter: put items on sale, set their price, manage gold reserves
Europa Universalis IV: official manual, monthly income from tax, production and trade

options.how: Build each room, hire individual doctors, nurses and handymen at negotiated salaries, and adjust what each treatment charges.
Zone land and set a tax rate; the yearly budget funds police, fire and transit as aggregate lines, with no individual firms.

sources.note: Theme Hospital: rooms, staff hiring and charges
SimCity: tax rate and yearly budget

options.how: Geo is the only money: spent at vendors, dropped on death and recovered by defeating your Shade.
Mora, Primogems, Genesis Crystals, Stardust and Starglitter each buy different things, including premium wishes.

sources.note: Hollow Knight: Geo, lost on death and recovered from the Shade
Genshin Impact: list of currencies including premium

options.how: One pool of dollars: earned by beating blinds plus $1 interest per $5 held (capped), all spent in the shop between rounds.
Gold from the rewards track buys packs and Arena runs, while Arcane Dust from disenchanting crafts specific cards.

sources.note: Balatro: money from blinds, interest, spent in the Shop
Hearthstone: gold earned on the rewards track, spent on packs and Arena
Hearthstone: Arcane Dust from disenchanting, spent crafting

options.how: Gold earned at your shop is the one currency; you manage the reserve and spend it on assistants and shop upgrades.
Bells buy most goods, while Nook Miles from activities unlock tickets, recipes, tool rings and pocket upgrades at the Nook Stop.

sources.note: Moonlighter: manage gold reserves, recruit assistants, upgrade the shop
Animal Crossing: New Horizons: Nook Miles spent at the Nook Stop, separate from Bells

options.how: Gold dug from the level is the only currency, amassed to buy armor and weapon upgrades.
Credits for general costs, Platinum on the market, Endo for mods, Ducats for Baro Ki'Teer, plus Standing with syndicates.

sources.note: Shovel Knight: amass riches to upgrade armor and weapons
Warframe: credits, platinum, ducats, standing and resource currencies

options.game: The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past
options.how: Rupees are the one currency, found in grass, pots and chests and spent at shops and minigames.
Gold, Elixir and Dark Elixir pay for different buildings and troops, while premium Gems speed up timers.

sources.note: The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past: Rupees as currency
Clash of Clans: gold, elixir, dark elixir and gems

options.how: Gold is the only currency: it drops from monsters, takes inventory space and buys gear and repairs from Tristram's townsfolk.
No gold: dozens of currency orbs, each a crafting consumable, serve as barter currency with vendors and players.

sources.note: Diablo: gold as the single currency
Path of Exile: currency items used for crafting and trade

options.how: Regional markets run on player buy and sell orders; most ships are player-built and destroyed for good when lost.
Since the gold and real-money auction houses shut on 18 March 2014, gear comes from drops and crafting, not player markets.

sources.note: EVE Online: regional markets of player buy and sell orders
Diablo III: auction houses closed 18 March 2014

options.how: Nearly every item is crafted by players and traded at local marketplaces in each city, so supply and prices are player-made.
Treasure is handed to NPC Trading Companies for gold, doubloons and reputation; there is no player-to-player market.

sources.note: Albion Online: nearly every item crafted by players, local marketplaces
Sea of Thieves: treasure exchanged with Trading Companies for gold and reputation

options.how: Players post Grand Exchange buy and sell offers at prices they choose; each offer starts from a guide price updated from trade history.
Gear comes from tiered loot drops, recipe crafting from salvaged components and faction vendors whose stock and discounts the designers set.

sources.note: Old School RuneScape: Grand Exchange offers at prices players choose
Grim Dawn: loot tiers, recipe crafting and faction vendor discounts

options.how: Players place vendors in their own houses and set the price of every item they stock, so shops are player-run.
No player trading: gear is forged at the Smithy from carved materials at designer-set costs.

sources.note: Ultima Online: player vendors in houses
Monster Hunter: World: forging gear from materials

options.how: Weapon skins drop or come from cases and trade on the Steam Community Market at prices players set.
Skins are bought only from Riot's in-game store at fixed prices and cannot be traded or resold.

sources.note: Counter-Strike: Global Offensive: skins traded on the Steam Community Market
Valorant: skins sold in the Riot store, no trading

options.how: Digital cards are tradeable between players, so collections are built through player trades and marketplaces.
Cards cannot be traded; wildcards from packs are redeemed for specific cards of the same rarity.

sources.note: Magic: The Gathering Online: official site, card trading
Magic: The Gathering Arena: official site, wildcard collection

options.how: NPC factions trade, build stations and wage war on their own, and ware prices drift with each station's stock.
Items have fixed base values; Speech skill and perks shift buy and sell rates, and each merchant has limited gold.

sources.note: X4: Foundations: factions trade, build and wage war independently
Skyrim: Speech skill modifies prices

options.how: A constantly changing shared market prices every resource as rivals produce, buy and sell; market moves replace weapons.
Every item has a set value; NPCs sell at it and buy back at one fifth, nudged only by NPC happiness and discount items.

sources.note: Offworld Trading Company: constantly changing market economy
Terraria: items sell for 1/5 of value, happiness modifies prices

options.how: Nook's Cranny turnip prices change every morning and afternoon, following one of four weekly patterns, from steady decline to a 600% spike.
Each fish species has a set base value per slot at the fishmonger; only trophy size and freshness change what a catch is worth.

sources.note: Animal Crossing: New Horizons: twice-daily turnip prices and weekly patterns
Dredge: fixed base value per fish, modified by size and condition

options.how: The Market trades wood, food and stone for gold, each 100-unit trade moves that price, and prices are shared by all players.
Shops sell items and mercenaries at fixed gold prices; economic levers are mining, lumber and upkeep, not prices.

sources.note: Age of Empires II: market prices change with each trade
Warcraft III: shop items at fixed gold costs

options.how: Hanseatic towns pay high prices for goods they lack, as in winter shortages, and little for surplus, so you buy where stock is high and sell where needed.
The fishmonger pays a fixed base price per species and slot; size and freshness are the only modifiers, so where and when you sell does not matter.

sources.note: Patrician III: trading empire, buying surplus and selling what towns need, winter shortage prices
Dredge: fixed base value per fish, modified by size and condition

options.how: Each town's prices follow local supply and demand, so caravans profit by hauling goods from surplus towns to scarce ones.
Poke Marts charge the same fixed price for each item everywhere, and items sell back for half.

sources.note: Mount & Blade II: Bannerlord: trade and fiefdom economy
Pokemon Red and Blue: fixed Poke Mart prices, items sell for half

options.how: Ammo and healing are scarce and inventory slots are few, so every shot and pickup is weighed.
Enemies and chests shower guns in rarity tiers; the choice is what to keep, sell or leave on the floor.

sources.note: Resident Evil 2 (2019): scarce ammo and limited inventory
Borderlands 3: loot rarity tiers

options.how: Night scavenging runs bring back little food or medicine for civilians short on both, so each trip decides who eats.
Randomized loot fills every level; your pet ferries surplus to town to sell so you can keep fighting.

sources.note: This War of Mine: scavenge for items while lacking food and medicine
Torchlight II: levels filled with loot, pet sells loot in town

options.how: Food, torches and shovels are bought before each expedition in capped stacks, and unused supplies refund at a steep loss.
Loot drops in common, magical, rare, epic and legendary classes; sorting the haul is a core activity.

sources.note: Darkest Dungeon: provisions bought before each dungeon, stack caps, reduced refunds
Grim Dawn: common to legendary classes of loot

options.how: Hunger, thirst and exhaustion drain constantly while resources run short, so you loot, barter, steal or beg for each day's needs.
Slain enemies drop the weapons they carried, and loot rolls from a pool of over 1,000 unique and legendary items.

sources.note: Pathologic 2: hunger, thirst, exhaustion and scarce resources; loot, barter, steal
Titan Quest: enemies drop their weapons; over 1,000 unique and legendary items

options.how: Ammo is scarce and nanites, the currency, are limited, so every replicator purchase and fight is rationed.
Monsters and chests drop gear in rarity tiers constantly; you sell or discard most of it.

sources.note: System Shock 2: nanites currency and scarce supplies
Titan Quest: item rarity tiers

options.how: Military-grade rounds are both the currency and the strongest ammo, so firing them spends your savings.
Enemies drop a steady stream of weapons and armor in rarity tiers; surplus is offered at shrines or sold.

sources.note: Metro 2033: military-grade ammunition as currency
Nioh: offering surplus gear at shrines

options.how: Currency orbs are both money and crafting consumables, so every craft destroys currency and drains the supply.
Gold has few uses beyond repairs and gambling, so it piles up and players barter with runes and rings instead.

sources.note: Path of Exile: currency items consumed in crafting and used to trade
Diablo II: gold uses and limits

note: Path of Exile option from the seed list; Diablo II counterpart added and not yet verified

options.how: Repair bills, training and respec fees, travel costs and huge vendor mounts and bank tabs keep pulling gold out of circulation.
Coins lie everywhere and only buy outfits, Power Moons and Life-Up Hearts at Crazy Cap; dying costs just 10 coins.

sources.note: World of Warcraft: repairs, training, respecs, travel and vendor gold sinks
Super Mario Odyssey: coins buy outfits, moons and hearts; 10 lost on death

note: World of Warcraft option from the seed list

options.how: Salaries must be paid on time and rations are always limited, so contract income has to keep outrunning the company's daily upkeep.
Cash and gold bars pile up while E. Gadd sells only a few 1,000 G items; the rebuilt hotel's look reflects how much you end with.

sources.note: Battle Brothers: salaries paid on time, rations always limited
Luigi's Mansion 3: money buys 1,000 G items; ending hotel depends on money

options.how: Bills arrive every few days based on what the household owns; leave them unpaid and the repo man takes furniture.
Gold collected in a run is also your score; shops are optional, so unspent gold simply accumulates.

sources.note: The Sims: bills and repossession
Spelunky: money as score and shop currency

options.how: Drills, assemblers and inserters linked by belts run production chains; you plan ratios so each line feeds the next.
Collect each resource from the ocean by hand and craft diving gear, habitat modules and subs from what you carry.

sources.note: Factorio: belts transport items placed by inserters
Subnautica: collect resources and craft gear, habitats and submersibles

options.how: Production chains of farms and factories deliver the goods each population tier needs before residents advance.
Pick twigs from saplings, chop logs and mine rocks yourself, then craft tools and structures from what you gathered.

sources.note: Anno 1800: complex production chains and population needs
Don't Starve: saplings picked by hand for twigs
Don't Starve: gather resources to craft items and structures

options.how: Factories run unattended; the AWESOME Sink turns surplus items into points that print FICSIT Coupons.
Throw a hook to catch floating debris by hand, then turn planks, plastic and leaves into tools and raft parts.

sources.note: Satisfactory: AWESOME Sink converts items to points for FICSIT Coupons
Raft: catch floating debris with your hook

options.how: Conveyor belts carry mined ore through supply chains that feed turrets and factories while you defend the core.
Swing a pickaxe to mine every block and ore yourself, then craft gear at crafting stations.

sources.note: Mindustry: supply chains of conveyor belts feeding turrets
Terraria: pickaxes mine blocks by hand

options.how: Settlers staff woodcutters, sawmills and smelters, so goods flow through the chain without you handling them.
Woodcutting, fishing and mining are gathering skills done one click at a time; you chop each tree yourself.

sources.note: The Settlers: automated production chains
RuneScape: Woodcutting is a gathering skill, click a tree to chop

options.how: Haul commodities between stations, buying where supply is high and selling where demand pays more.
Drop goods in the shipping bin and they sell overnight at fixed prices; there is no buy-low, sell-high loop.

sources.note: Elite Dangerous: fully realised economy for trade
Stardew Valley: shipping bin sells overnight

options.how: Set up trade routes among 60 Caribbean cities, buying goods where they are cheap to supply other towns' growing needs.
Loot is sold to vendors almost as an afterthought, and your pet can make the run to town for you; no resale loop exists.

sources.note: Port Royale 4: trade routes across the Caribbean, 60 cities
Torchlight II: pet runs to town to sell your loot

options.how: Buy stock cheaply in town markets and resell it in your own shop at a markup, setting the price for every sale.
Gold dug from levels is spent on armor and weapon upgrades; there is nothing to buy low and sell high.

sources.note: Recettear: playing the markets in town, deciding sale prices
Shovel Knight: amass riches to upgrade armor and weapons

options.how: Buy commodities in one system and sell them in another, where agricultural and industrial economies price goods differently.
Loot wrecks and craft equipment between runs; there is no commodity trading loop.

sources.note: Elite: commodity trading between systems
Everspace: shoot, craft and loot

options.how: Load cargo at one base and sell it at another, choosing between trading, bounty hunting and piracy for income.
Scrap from fights buys upgrades and fuel at stores; selling spare gear is a sideline, not a loop.

sources.note: Wing Commander: Privateer: cargo trading between bases
FTL: scrap earned and spent at stores

options.how: Everything you produce can be sold on the shared market, and buying up rivals' supply is a main lever.
Workers harvest minerals and gas straight into your bank; there is no market or trading at all.

sources.note: Offworld Trading Company: market forces as weapons, goods to build and sell
StarCraft: minerals and vespene gas

options.how: Every good must be delivered: you build rail, road, water and air lines to carry raw materials to factories and finished goods to cities.
Each business pays its profits straight into one cash balance that buys upgrades and more businesses at once; nothing is shipped or stored.

sources.note: Transport Fever 2: deliver raw materials and goods through economic chains
AdVenture Capitalist: businesses earn profits that buy upgrades and more businesses

options.how: Goods move by truck, train, ship, pipe and conveyor between storage and factories; long distances need vehicles.
Every planet's output joins one empire-wide stockpile, spendable anywhere the instant it is produced.

sources.note: Workers & Resources: vehicles essential for moving resources long distances
Stellaris: empire-wide resource stockpile

options.how: Carriers walk every good flag to flag along roads you build; a jammed road starves the next building.
Villagers carry loads to a drop site, but once delivered resources join one pool any building can spend.

sources.note: The Settlers: carriers on road segments
Age of Empires II: resources dropped off into a shared stockpile

options.how: Trains carry cargo and passengers between stations you connect; revenue depends on route, distance and demand.
Peons bring gold and lumber to a town hall, where it pools and pays for anything anywhere on the map.

sources.note: Railroad Tycoon: trains hauling cargo between stations
Warcraft II: gold and lumber returned to the town hall

options.how: Materials must be transported and processed through production chains, and resources scattered across the map push you to found specialized settlements.
Every building, from Cursors and Grandmas to Portals, adds cookies straight into one bank that pays for anything at once.

sources.note: Manor Lords: materials transported and processed through production chains
Cookie Clicker: buildings produce cookies automatically into one total

options.how: Every delivery is carried on your back or in a vehicle; weight and balance shape the route and what you can bring.

options.game: Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain
options.how: Fulton balloons send materials and recruits to Mother Base, where they become instantly usable resources.

sources.note: Death Stranding: cargo weight and balance
Metal Gear Solid V: Fulton extraction to Mother Base

options.how: Platinum is sold for real money and can be traded to other players for tradable items such as Prime parts and mods.
All heroes are free and the core content is open to everyone; spending real money only buys cosmetics and add-ons.

sources.note: Warframe: Platinum bought with real money and tradable between players
Dota 2: all heroes free, cosmetics only

options.how: Eternal Orbs are bought with real money and turn into Legendary Crests that boost rift rewards.
The store sells cosmetics and stash tabs; currency orbs come only from play and trading.

sources.note: Diablo Immortal: Eternal Orbs as premium currency
Path of Exile: official shop sells cosmetics and stash tabs

options.how: Players post buy and sell orders on each settlement's Trading Post; the settlement sets listing fees and purchase taxes.
Weapons and armor are forged by turning monster materials in to the Smithy; surplus materials only trade to the Buddy Smithy for Scraps.

sources.note: New World: player buy and sell orders, settlement fees and taxes
Monster Hunter Rise: Smithy forges gear from turned-in monster materials

options.how: Gold drains into Abbey and Tavern stress relief, provisions, blacksmith upgrades, skill training and Sanitarium quirk removal.
Coins from battles and blocks buy items and badges at shops and cap at 999, with no upkeep or recurring costs.

sources.note: Darkest Dungeon: gold spent on stress relief, provisions, upgrades, skills, Sanitarium
Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door: coins buy items and badges, 999 cap

options.how: Run convoys between Hanseatic ports, buying goods where they are in surplus and selling where towns need them, to grow a trading empire.
Gold gathered during runs only buys permanent power-ups between runs; there is nothing to sell and no market.

sources.note: Patrician III: massive trading operations across Hanseatic ports
Vampire Survivors: gather gold in each run to buy upgrades

options.how: Bonds are bought from Jagex with real money, sold to other players for coins on the Grand Exchange or redeemed for membership.
Sold once with paid expansions and no microtransactions, so GP and items can only be earned by playing.

sources.note: Old School RuneScape: bonds bought with real money, tradeable for coins
Melvor Idle: does not contain microtransactions

options.how: Mammoth Coins come only from real-money purchases and buy Legends and cosmetics; free Gold from matches and missions buys less.
Gold is earned in solo modes, matches and challenges and spent in the shop or on Classic Mode continues.

sources.note: Brawlhalla: Mammoth Coins only from real money; Gold has no real-money option
Super Smash Bros. Ultimate: gold from solo modes and challenges, spent in the shop

options.how: Runestones come only from paid Runestone Bundles and can buy any product in the shop, down to single Battlegrounds hero skins.
A one-time purchase with expansions and no microtransactions; every currency comes from training skills and play.

sources.note: Hearthstone: Runestones only from paid bundles
Melvor Idle: does not contain microtransactions

options.how: Goods move between production buildings and specialized settlements spread over a map of scattered resources, so distance shapes supply.
Resource buildings collect from the surrounding land straight into the colony's shared stock, so no one hauls or stores goods.

sources.note: Manor Lords: materials transported between production chains, resources spread across the map
They Are Billions: collect resources from the environment using building structures

options.how: Opening a business means taking a loan, renting a building and hiring staff, so rent, repayments and wages keep draining cash.
Gold buys permanent power-ups, but refunding them is free, so spent gold is never truly lost and reallocating costs nothing.

sources.note: Big Ambitions: take out a loan, rent a building, hire staff
Vampire Survivors: gold buys upgrades; refunding power-ups is free
